world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Koyra Chiini (koyr1240) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had one title, Glottolog 60264 = Nicolaï 1982 in SAL 13(3) (Glottolog's title conflates it with the 1978 segmental article; the 1982 paper is 'Problèmes de dynamique linguistique: recherches en prosodie songhay', pp. 273-322, a reworking of ch. VI of his thesis). The full issue is open access and was already held by the project; I verified the two relevant passages against page renders (p. 281 Type 1; pp. 307-308 sec. 23) and saved the renders, the Glottolog record and the SAL landing page there with a entry. The statement: Western Songhay (Tombouctou/Djenné/Araouan) has a fixed accent on the last long syllable, else on the final syllable, with no surviving pitch/accent contrasts. This is a one-sentence typological summary, hedged, no examples. The best descriptive source remains Heath 1999 A Grammar of Koyra Chiini sec. 3.9.2 (Mouton, DOI 10.1515/9783110804850; only Google Books snippets reachable, held by the project), which says stress is nonphonemic and phonetically reduced on final syllables -- at odds with Nicolaï's final-syllable default; acquiring Heath 1999 in full stays the high-priority gap for this language (not a works with stress in the title).

new_statements.quote: [p.47] Type 1 : Système prosodique à accent fixe qui semble tomber soit sur la dernière syllabe longue du 'mot' soit sur la syllabe finale si le 'mot' ne possède pas de syllabe longue. Ce type a été relevé dans le songhay occidental. [p.40] ... les parlers du songhay occidental, à savoir les parlers de la région de Tombouctou, Djenné, Ngorku ... [pp.329-330] 6.5.2.6. Le songhay occidental. Dans ce dialecte la confusion entre les schèmes prosodiques est complète; les distinctions qui subsistent en songhay septentrional et en songhay oriental n'existent pas. L'actualisation de cette confusion implique que l'opposition de hauteur a été neutralisée sans que l'intensité ait pu servir de trait de transfert pour soutenir les distinctions résiduelles.
new_statements.translation: [p.47] Type 1: a prosodic system with fixed accent, which seems to fall either on the last long syllable of the 'word', or on the final syllable if the 'word' has no long syllable. This type has been recorded in Western Songhay. [p.40] ... the Western Songhay varieties, namely those of the region of Timbuktu, Djenné, Ngorku ... [pp.329-330] 6.5.2.6. Western Songhay. In this dialect the merger of the prosodic schemas is complete; the distinctions that survive in Northern Songhay and Eastern Songhay do not exist. This merger implies that the pitch opposition was neutralised without intensity being able to serve as a transfer feature to support the residual distinctions.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Koyra Chiini (Nicolaï's 'songhay occidental': Timbuktu, Djenné, Ngorku) has lost lexical tone entirely and has only a non-distinctive, predictable word accent: it falls on the rightmost syllable containing a long vowel, and on the word-final syllable when the word has no long syllable (Nicolaï hedges with 'semble tomber'). Nicolaï 1982/1983 restates: no tonal realisation at all, only a fixed accent predictable from segmental structure and word boundaries.
new_statements.exceptions: None given; the rule itself is hedged ('qui semble tomber'). Nicolaï notes a potential Tombouctou vs 'extrême-occidental' (Djenné, Ngorku) split only for segmental features (palatalisation of /s/), not for accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological 'mot' (Nicolaï's quotes around 'mot'); accent is explicitly non-distinctive (all inherited prosodic schemas merged). Statement is typological/summary in nature, based on Nicolaï's own fieldwork with Timbuktu and Djenné speakers (in Niamey and in Mali); no worked examples with accent marks are given for this dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Nicolaï's unit is 'songhay occidental' = the Songhay varieties of Tombouctou (Timbuktu), Djenné and Ngorku, i.e. Glottolog koyr1240 Koyra Chiini Songhay including its dialects koyr1241 (Koyra Chiini proper, Timbuktu/Goundam) and djen1242 (Djenné Chiini). He notes a possible Tombouctou vs 'extrême-occidental' (Djenné, Ngorku/Jimbala) split for segmental features only. Prost 1956 (also saved) describes Gao Songhay = koyr1242 and must not be used for this key.

new_statements.translation: Type 1: prosodic system with fixed accent, which seems to fall either on the last long syllable of the 'word' or on the final syllable if the 'word' has no long syllable. This type was recorded in Western Songhay.
new_statements.citation: Nicolaï, Robert. 1982. Problèmes de dynamique linguistique: recherches en prosodie songhay. Studies in African Linguistics 13(3): 273-322 (DOI of the full issue 10.32473/sal.v13i3.107604).
new_statements.locator: p. 281 (PDF p. 69), sec. 4 typology, 'Type 1'; supporting sec. 23 'Le songhay occidental' pp. 307-308; appendix II p. 314 ('Songhay Occidental' = Djenné, Tombouctou, Araouan)
new_statements.reading: Fixed, non-contrastive, weight-sensitive word accent: rightmost heavy (long-vowel) syllable; default final syllable when the word has no heavy syllable (an unbounded right-oriented quantity-sensitive pattern). Hedged ('semble'), given without examples, and derived from Nicolaï's 1979/1981 thesis rather than a dedicated description. Heath 1999's grammar (sec. 3.9.2, seen only in Google Books snippets held by the project) instead calls stress nonphonemic with reduced phonetic stress on final syllables, so a catalog entry built on Nicolaï should flag Heath as a dissenting first-hand source and the language as a weak/uncertain fixed-stress case.

sources.note: Western Songhay (Tombouctou/Djenné/Araouan = Koyra Chiini and Djenné Chiini) is the one Songhay variety with a fixed, predictable accent: it falls on the last long (heavy) syllable of the word, else on the final syllable; no tonal or accentual contrasts survive there (complete neutralisation of the Proto-Songhay pitch opposition). This is a whole-family comparative/diachronic paper; the Western Songhay statement is a one-sentence typological summary (hedged 'semble') plus a short diachronic section, not a full description with examples.
